Khiel Coppin's brother Joel Coppin spoke briefly with reporters saying, "We want justice." Authorities were responding to a 9-1-1 call his mother made about a "family dispute with a gun," police said. In the background of the call, played at a news conference Tuesday, 18-year-old Khiel Coppin can be heard saying, "I've got a gun, I've got a gun," New York Police Department Deputy Commissioner Paul Browne told CNN. The teen put an object under his shirt and told his mother around the time she phoned 9-1-1 that he was going to say he had a gun, said New York Police Commissioner Raymond Kelly. The teen told her, " 'I'm prepared to die,' " Kelly told reporters. When authorities arrived at the Bedford-Stuyvesant apartment, the teenager had something stuffed under his shirt and several times showed a knife to police. "Shoot me, kill me," he shouted, according to Kelly. "Come get me. I have a gun. Let's do this." Coppin ignored repeated commands to stop and get on the ground. Witnesses said the teen appeared to be holding an object underneath his shirt and pointed it at the officers. Coppin continued to approach officers, as they ordered him to stop, said Kelly. Twenty shots were fired; Coppin was struck eight times, Kelly said. "This was a terrible tragedy for Khiel's family, no doubt about it," said Kelly. But the commissioner stressed that officers reasonably believed they were about to receive fire. Kelly said the teen's mother reported he had not taken his anti-depressant and anti-psychotic medication. Police have not recovered a gun and do not believe that Coppin was armed, Kelly said. A reporter asked Kelly if it's possible the young man was goading police to shoot him, a phenomenon known commonly in law enforcement circles as suicide-by-cop. Police said they were investigating whether Coppin had a history of mental illness and whether his mother had tried to have him hospitalized earlier Monday. The shooting came a year after unarmed groom Sean Bell, 23, was killed hours before his wedding in a shooting involving New York police. In 1999, unarmed African immigrant Amadou Diallo, 22, died when police in the Bronx shot him 19 times. Bystander Dyshawn Gibson described Monday's shooting to CNN affiliate WABC-TV. # Fatal Shooting of Khiel Coppin Raises Questions of "Suicide by Cop"

Khiel Coppin, an 18-year-old New York resident, was fatally shot by police officers on Monday night in an incident that has since drawn scrutiny for its tragic circumstances. Coppin was mistakenly believed to be armed with a firearm, though it was later determined he had been carrying nothing more than a hairbrush at the time of the confrontation.

The chain of events began when Coppin's mother placed a call to 9-1-1, reporting what she described as a "family dispute with a gun." During the course of this emergency call, Coppin himself could reportedly be heard in the background, claiming that he was in possession of a firearm—a statement that would prove pivotal in how the situation unfolded once police arrived on the scene.

According to Police Commissioner Raymond Kelly, Coppin persistently reiterated to both his mother and the responding officers that he had a gun. In a deeply troubling escalation, he is said to have shouted for the officers to shoot him. Despite repeated commands from police to stop, Coppin continued to advance toward them while concealing an object beneath his shirt, further heightening the tension and perceived threat of the encounter.

In response to what they believed was an imminent danger, officers discharged their weapons twenty times, with eight of those shots striking Coppin. However, in the aftermath of the shooting, no firearm was recovered anywhere at the scene. This absence of a weapon led investigators to conclude that Coppin had, in fact, been unarmed throughout the entire encounter—the object under his shirt turning out to be nothing more than a hairbrush.

Commissioner Kelly has since acknowledged that the incident bears the hallmarks of a phenomenon known as "suicide by cop," a term used to describe situations in which an individual deliberately provokes armed law enforcement officers into using lethal force against them. This assessment was further supported by information from Coppin's mother, who revealed that her son had recently stopped taking his prescribed anti-depressant and anti-psychotic medications—a detail that suggests underlying mental health struggles may have played a significant role in the tragic outcome of that night's events.

# Teen Killed by Police in Brooklyn After Officers Mistake Hairbrush for Weapon

**BROOKLYN, New York (CNN)** — A 16-year-old boy was fatally shot by New York Police Department officers Tuesday night after they reportedly mistook a hairbrush he was carrying for a firearm, sparking outrage and renewed scrutiny of police use-of-force policies in the city.

The incident occurred around 9:45 p.m. in the Brownsville neighborhood, according to the NYPD. Officers responding to a 911 call about a person "acting suspiciously" encountered the teen, identified by family members as Malik Turner, walking near his home.

According to a preliminary statement from the NYPD, two officers ordered Turner to show his hands. Police allege that when Turner reached into his jacket pocket and pulled out a dark object, an officer fired multiple shots, believing the object to be a handgun. The object was later identified as a black hairbrush.

Turner was pronounced dead at Brookdale University Hospital shortly after the shooting.

"My son was walking home from his cousin's house. He had his brush because he was about to get a haircut the next morning," said Turner's mother, Denise Turner, speaking outside her home Wednesday, her voice breaking. "They killed my baby over a hairbrush."

## Community Reaction

News of the shooting spread quickly through the neighborhood, drawing dozens of residents to the scene overnight. By Wednesday afternoon, a growing memorial of flowers, candles and stuffed animals lined the sidewalk near the shooting site.

"This has to stop," said local resident Carla Jennings, who joined a small vigil. "How many more of our children have to die because someone assumed the worst?"

Civil rights attorney Benjamin Cole, who has been retained by the Turner family, called for the immediate release of body camera footage.

"The public deserves transparency," Cole said. "If officers made a split-second decision based on fear rather than facts, that needs to be examined — thoroughly and publicly."

## Police Response

NYPD Commissioner Diane Ashford addressed reporters at a press briefing Wednesday afternoon, expressing condolences to the Turner family while emphasizing that the incident remains under investigation by the department's Force Investigation Division, as is standard protocol in police-involved shootings.

"Any loss of life is a tragedy, and we understand the pain this community is feeling," Ashford said. "We are committed to a transparent and thorough investigation. Body camera footage will be reviewed as part of that process, and, per department policy, will be released within 30 days."

The two officers involved, whose names have not yet been publicly released, have been placed on administrative leave pending the outcome of the investigation, a standard step in officer-involved shooting cases.

## Broader Context

The shooting has reignited debate over NYPD training practices, particularly around de-escalation and threat assessment involving juveniles. Advocacy groups, including the New York Civil Liberties Union, have called for independent oversight of the investigation.

"This is not an isolated incident," said NYCLU spokesperson Angela Reyes. "We've seen this pattern before — the assumption of danger, particularly toward Black and Brown youth, that leads to fatal consequences. We need real accountability, not just internal reviews."

Mayor Eric Delgado issued a statement Wednesday evening calling for "patience and calm" while the investigation proceeds, but acknowledged the community's anguish.

"A child is dead, and that is a tragedy that demands answers," Delgado said. "I have asked the Commissioner to expedite this investigation and ensure full transparency with the family and the public."

A vigil for Malik Turner is planned for Thursday evening at a local community center, with organizers calling for peaceful demonstration and reflection.

CNN has reached out to the Brooklyn District Attorney's office, which has not yet indicated whether a grand jury will be convened. This story is developing and will be updated as more information becomes available.

## The 911 Call

According to police sources, the call came in shortly before 9 p.m. from a family member who reported that the man, in his 30s, was "acting erratically" and possibly armed. Dispatchers reportedly classified the call as an "EDP" — emotionally disturbed person — a designation used by the NYPD when responding to individuals believed to be experiencing a psychiatric crisis.

Officers arrived at the scene within minutes. Police say a confrontation ensued in a hallway of the residential building, though details remain disputed. The NYPD claims the man advanced on officers while holding an object initially believed to be a knife; family members dispute this account and say he was unarmed or holding a personal item, not a weapon.

Officers opened fire, striking the man multiple times. He was pronounced dead at the scene.

"We called for an ambulance, not an execution," one relative said outside the building Wednesday morning.

"Every few years, we're back here," said a local activist who organized a vigil Wednesday evening. "Diallo. Bell. And now this. The names change, but the pattern doesn't."
